title: It is I (Mark 6:45–52)
hookLine: walking on the lake at night: take heart, it is I, do not be afraid

lines: ALONE ON THE HILL TO PRAY.
cards: Straight after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples off in the boat ahead of him, sends the crowd home, and climbs a hill alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the lake, the wind turns against them.
They row, and row, and get nowhere. Hours of it, arms burning, the shore not getting any closer. Some problems are like that: rowing since sundown, getting nowhere.
Then, in the last watch of the night, someone sees a figure on the water. Walking.

teach.h: HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.
teach.b: In the old King James Bible: "he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them: and about the fourth watch of the night he cometh unto them, walking upon the sea, and would have passed by them."
He saw them. From the hill, in the dark, he's been watching them struggle. The fourth watch is the last stretch of the night, before dawn.

teach.h: HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY THEM.
teach.b: Then a strange phrase: he would have passed by them. Readers take it in different ways. Some hear an echo of the old stories where God passes by Moses on the mountain and Elijah at the cave, showing himself as he goes.
The disciples think it's a ghost, and they scream. He speaks at once: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." Take heart.
It is I. Don't be afraid.

teach.h: IT IS I — EGO EIMI, I AM.
teach.b: In Greek, it is I is two words, ego eimi, which can also mean simply, I am. Some Christians hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush: I am. Then he climbs into the boat, and the wind stops.

Mark gives us something more honest: they were utterly astonished, "For they considered not the miracle of the loaves: for their heart was hardened." They'd just seen five thousand fed, and it hadn't sunk in.
And Mark's version has no Peter stepping out onto the water; that's in Matthew. Here it's just Jesus, the dark, the wind, and three phrases for frightened people.

how: Christians often turn to this story in times of fear or long struggle, and some pray its words, be of good cheer, be not afraid, for people facing a long night.

games.q: it's nearly dawn. you've rowed all night against the wind. a figure is walking toward you across the water. what do you do?
games.why: they cry out, thinking it's a spirit. he answers at once: be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid.

practice: Picture someone rowing against the wind right now, a friend with a long night behind them and more ahead, someone whose arms are tired, and hold them in mind. Imagine standing near them and saying, simply, take heart.
If you pray, you can pray the words from the story for them: be of good cheer, be not afraid.
